text:
E0: THE IDENTITY ANOMALY WAS MINE, AND IT IS FULLY EXPLAINED.

The earlier reading said two NodeServices looked like one object and their
AddressManager was not the instance captured moments before. Measured
precisely, with all normal setup and reset first and nothing reset between the
observations:

  construction                         new NodeService(...)
  nodeA !== nodeB                      true
  nodeA.constructor === NodeService    true
  nodeB.constructor === NodeService    true

So A1's direct-construction invariant is intact; nothing routed through
NodeService.getInstance(). The earlier appearance of sameness was that both
nodeAddress fields read null.

The reason is one line of reading order. nodeId, nodeAddress and
addressManager are assigned in initialize(), not in the constructor, so the
first witness compared fields that nothing had set yet - undefined against
undefined for the two nodes, and undefined against the captured manager. After
initializing both with explicit ids and addresses:

  nodeA.addressManager === manager0              true
  nodeB.addressManager === manager0              true
  nodeA.addressManager === nodeB.addressManager  true
  constructor === AddressManager                 true
  manager0.constructor === theirs.constructor    true
  AddressManager.resetInstance calls after capture  0

Neither E1 branch applies. There was no reset between capture and use - proved
by counting calls to resetInstance around the window rather than by inspection
- and there are not two module graphs: the constructor identities are the
same object. One module, one singleton, two distinct node runtimes sharing it.

Repaired in the witness only. No production source was touched, and the
anomaly says nothing about AddressManager's authority either way.

ADDRESSMANAGER SEALED GREEN, WITH NO PRODUCTION SOURCE CHANGE.

THE ADVERSARIAL SETUP, on real production objects in both peer-bearing
subsystems. The node's own authoritative cache says the peer is at A; the
process-global registry is poisoned toward B - cleared, then filled with the
poison node and the poison address, and with nothing naming A. A is
node-a/.../r2 and B is node-evil/.../r2. The registry is poisoned before the
peer is joined AND again immediately before the write, because the destination
is resolved twice: once at join and once at send.

PARTITION PATH, through the real PartitionService.

  cache authoritative, registry poisoned toward B        -> A
  already-unified A, registry poisoned toward B          -> A
  no authoritative location, registry holds B            -> REFUSES
  terminal: peer slot after initialize()                 RemotePeerRepresentation at A
  terminal: destination the production write reached     A

MESSAGE-GROUP PATH, through a real MessageGroupService on a real MessageRouter
(its transport-shape check is satisfied by the real router; deliver is
observed and delegated, never replaced by a harness routing table).

  cache authoritative, registry poisoned toward B        -> A
  already-unified A, registry poisoned toward B          -> A
  no authoritative location, registry holds B            -> REFUSES
  bootstrap hints explicitly permitted                   -> A, from the hint
                                                            list, not the registry
  terminal: peer slot after initialize()                 RemotePeerRepresentation at A
  terminal: destination the production write reached     A

TWO RUNTIMES, ONE REGISTRY, NO RESET. Two real PartitionService runtimes on
different nodes, verified sharing one AddressManager instance across the
observations. The shared registry was then cleared, re-filled with a
conflicting claim about node-b's peer, and node-b's peer address unregistered.
Both nodes' actual write destinations were unchanged. A mutation made under
node-a did not move node-b's destination.

WHY, AT THE LEVEL OF WHAT PRODUCTION CALLS. Production uses exactly seven
AddressManager methods:

  format                 25 sites   argument-only
  parse                  14 sites   argument-only
  validate               11 sites   argument-only
  generateNodeAddress     1 site    uuid + set insert
  generateServiceAddress  1 site    uuid + set insert
  unregisterNodeAddress   1 site
  unregisterServiceAddress 1 site

and there is ZERO production reference - not merely zero calls - to
hasNodeAddressConflict, hasServiceAddressConflict, hasAddressConflict,
getAllNodeAddresses, getAllServiceAddresses, getNodeAddressCount or
getServiceAddressCount outside address-manager.js itself. Conflict detection
is read only by registerNodeAddress and registerServiceAddress, and neither
has a production caller. Both generators are unconditional: neither consults
hasAddressConflict. So the mutable registry is written and unwritten, and
nothing reads it back to decide anything.

THE FINDING, bounded to what was measured:

  AddressManager's mutable process-global registry is observationally inert
  for peer-location decisions in the measured formation proof cone.

  Production peer resolution derives location from explicit unified addresses
  and authoritative runtime/cache state.

  AddressManager contributes parsing, validation and formatting.

  When authoritative location is absent, the tested paths fail closed rather
  than promote registry membership into discovery authority.

It is NOT claimed that AddressManager is harmless globally, nor that it never
affects semantics. The proof is bounded to the formation paths above.

NO INJECTION SEAM WAS ADDED BECAUSE NO SEMANTIC LEAK WAS DEMONSTRATED. No
AddressManager.getInstance() call site was swept, no API was deleted - dead or
unused cleanup is not this frontier - and no production source was changed at
all. That is a positive architectural result: the global-looking
implementation is not, on these paths, a global-acting one.

WHAT MAKES IT DURABLE. The witness is committed, and its last assertion is the
standing claim rather than a single run: it walks src/ and requires that no
production file outside address-manager.js so much as mentions a registry-read
API. A future caller that made the registry an authority would turn it red
before it could become a defect.

INVARIANTS REMEASURED AT THE SEAL:

  ownerAddressCount 138, peerObjectCount 276, peerAddressCount 138
  runtimesInPeerSlots [], authorityBreaches []
  peer write 16,334, end 138, peer probe 0
  strict violations 0, substitutions 0, eligible true
  F probe 0; census productionSemanticUnowned 0, unknown 0, ambiguous 0,
    peer/carrier owner assignments 0, overlap 0, partition delta 0
  afterTeardown pending 0, postSealProductionEffects 0, postSealEnqueues 0
  formation-sim-reproduces: the same 3 unmet predicates

GATES. Static green with every ratchet at its baseline. The canonical corpus
was run, per the E process lesson, rather than a cone chosen by me: 2 failures
of the whole corpus, and they are exactly the two inherited deliberate reds
classified under F - dt6-formation-ledger-quorum-spread-first and
dt6-voter-surplus-promotion-drain-livelock - unmodified and belonging to other
quests. The movielens cohort test that E had regressed is green.

ONE WORKTREE NOTE, recorded because it cost a full gate cycle: a fresh git
worktree has no node_modules and no generated import graph, and both make the
canonical gates fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the change. The
sibling worktree symlinks node_modules to the main checkout; the import graph
is regenerated with generate-global-owner-debt-inventory.js
--refresh-import-graph-only.

NOT FORCED THROUGH SOLVE LAND, for the same reason F is frozen. Probe 0 and every gate green; the canonical corpus has exactly two failures, both inherited deliberate reds owned by other open quests (dt6-formation-ledger-quorum-spread-first, dt6-voter-surplus-promotion-drain-livelock), both red on the pre-F baseline and untouched here. No inherited-red waiver is taken: neither test is modified, excluded, baselined or bypassed, and this quest is marked neither solved nor terminal-blocked. When the owning quests make the corpus green, return to this checkpoint on quest/address-manager and perform an ordinary solve land.

Ruled out: the process-global AddressManager registry is not a peer-location authority on the measured formation paths - PartitionService and MessageGroupService peer resolution, including two runtimes sharing one registry. Poisoning the registry changed no peer-location decision and no destination a production write reached, and with no authoritative location those paths refuse (adversarial witness in 73e8f8446, on main since the 2026-09-17 merge 90f21f0e5; probe address-manager-peer-location-authority.js 0 at main ba7068036). The claim is bounded to those paths; it is not that AddressManager is harmless globally.

Superseded: the frontier closed with no leak to repair, so there is nothing to land. The statement already held when this record was written: on the measured formation paths (PartitionService and MessageGroupService peer resolution, including two runtimes sharing one registry), poisoning the process-global AddressManager registry changed no peer-location decision and no destination a production write reached, and with no authoritative location those paths refuse. A quest cannot be born satisfied, so solve never sealed it; its probe (address-manager-peer-location-authority.js) was green when the record was committed in 73e8f8446, on main since the 2026-09-17 merge 90f21f0e5. What is superseded is the suspicion that the registry is a peer-location authority on these paths; the adversarial witness refuted it. Re-run at main ba7068036: probe 0. The witness and probe stay on main as evidence; the claim is bounded to the measured paths and is not that AddressManager is harmless globally. No production change was made and none is claimed.
